results.title: Putin's handshake, fried chicken and high-stakes diplomacy
results.description: Putin's handshake, fried chicken and high-stakes diplomacy melissa_fernan… Thu, 19 Nov 2026 - 09:55 US President Donald Trump arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of the highest-stakes leg of his Asia trip: an unprecedented summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The gathering in Shenzhen brings together the leaders of the world's three biggest nuclear powers at a moment of tension over Ukraine, Iran, trade and a global arms buildup. Here are some takeaways from Trump's second full day in the region. A WEIGHTY HANDSHAKE A gathering of world leaders inevitably involves plenty of handshakes, but one in particular stood out on Wednesday. Putin approached Trump and initiated a handshake in front of cameras, offering a public display of cordiality between the two leaders at a time when Russia remains isolated from much of the West over its war in Ukraine. The moment gave Putin an opportunity to show that he retains direct access to the American president and remains a player on the world stage. For Trump, it reflected his emphasis on personal relationships with other world leaders. The brief exchange did not guarantee any policy breakthroughs but set a friendly tone ahead of Thursday, when Trump, Putin and Xi are scheduled to hold the first trilateral meeting among the three leaders. Trump is also expected to meet Putin separately. The leaders' agendas for the meeting do not entirely align. Trump wants to talk about limiting nuclear weapons, a subject that Xi would prefer to avoid because his country is engaged in a massive nuclear buildup to catch up with US and Russian dominance. Trump has also said Ukraine and Iran will come up. In opening remarks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, Putin criticized Western sanctions imposed over Russia's war in Ukraine, while Xi took aim at US tariffs, calling for "free and open trade." A PRESIDENT WHO LOVES THE STAGE Trump has a way of making even a routine arrival look different from those of other world leaders. As leaders entered the APEC summit banquet, most walked past an eight-piece classical music ensemble and a throng of journalists with little more than a nod or passing glance. Trump took a different approach. As the band played "America the Beautiful," he paused for roughly 10 seconds, appearing to take in the music before turning directly toward the press corps and facing the cameras. He held the pose, giving photographers a straight-on portrait shot that stood out from the procession of more understated arrivals. It was a small but unmistakably Trump moment. He has long embraced the pageantry of the presidency, relishing military jet flyovers, crisp salutes and elaborate welcome dances — all with him at center stage. FRIED CHICKEN DIPLOMACY Trump's love of fast food is well documented. One of the most memorable photos from his winning 2024 presidential campaign captured him wearing an apron and cooking french fries at a McDonald's. On Wednesday, Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced to a gathering of Asian leaders in Manila that he had ordered fried chicken from the famed Filipino chain Jollibee for Trump and his delegation as a late-night snack. Marcos boasted that Jollibee is so popular that "we are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity." "Oh wow, fantastic," said Trump, who has been known to dip into buckets of the US chain's fried poultry. It was unclear whether he ate any of the Jollibee delivery. A QUICK HELLO WITH A LONGTIME FRIEND Trump's Manila visit included a reunion with Imelda Marcos, the 97-year-old former first lady whose husband, Ferdinand Marcos, governed the Philippines for 21 years before being driven from power in 1986. Her vast collection of jewels and more than 1,000 pairs of shoes became a symbol of the family's excess during his autocratic rule. Now the Marcos family is back in power with her son, known widely as Bongbong, serving as president. Sitting in a wheelchair, Imelda Marcos blew Trump a kiss during their brief encounter, shared in a video posted on social media by a White House aide. "Have a good time, okay?" Trump told her. The two go back decades. Trump met the former first lady at a New York party when he was a rising real estate developer and recalled his long history with the family earlier in the trip. “I just don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well, and they were great," Trump told Marcos Jr. in a speech on Tuesday night. "I believe in genetics, and they did a good job. You have very good genetics. I can tell you that." DEALS NOW, DETAILS LATER Trump has repeatedly used his Asia trip to declare economic victories, an important message for a president whose tariff policies have faced criticism at home over their effect on prices and whose Republican Party suffered major losses in the November midterm elections. Eager to show he is making progress, Trump twice on the trip has announced what he portrayed as significant trade breakthroughs, with Thailand and the Philippines. "This is an incredible victory," Trump said of the Thai agreement. The details, however, are not completely sorted. A White House statement on the Thai deal said the two governments had reached a "substantial conclusion" and that final work toward an agreement would now be made. Trump said under the pending deal, Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports and remove substantial non-tariff barriers. Trump called the Philippines agreement a landmark deal that would benefit US farmers and the energy sector, though he provided no specific terms, figures or timeline. Manila said the two countries had reached only an understanding on economic cooperation. TRUMP X FACTOR For all the anticipation leading up to Thursday's three-way summit, expectations for a major breakthrough are low. Trump, Xi and Putin are coming to the table with different priorities. The Chinese leader wants to focus generally on world peace, Putin is looking for an off-ramp out of the war in Ukraine on favorable terms and Trump would like to limit nuclear weapons. The meeting is expected to be highly choreographed, with access tightly controlled. But at such a high-profile gathering, there is a certain degree of unpredictability about what Trump might do when the cameras are rolling. Ukrainian and European leaders are nervous that Trump might try to strike a deal with Putin on Ukraine. Taiwan is worried about any move by the leaders that could encourage China to put more pressure on the self-ruled island. The summit may be scripted. Trump often isn't. Stay tuned. results.title: 'Capitalism Has Declared War On Democracy': Stewart's Podcast Goes Off The Rails
results.description: 'Capitalism Has Declared War On Democracy': Stewart's Podcast Goes Off The Rails Comedy Central’s Jon Stewart welcomed The Nerd Reich: Big Tech, Trump & Fascism author Gil Durán to his Wednesday episode of The Weekly Show podcast, and with a book title like that, the flood of Nazi and fascist accusations that followed was wild, but not unexpected. At one point Stewart wondered about tech elites, “This a purposeful threat to democracy, yes? Like, have they made specific moves that you consider, kind of, anti-democratic? You know, a sort of explicit revelation of their motivation.” On multiple occasions, Durán would accuse tech giants, such as Elon Musk, of anti-democratic behavior for things liberals do all the time. On this occasion, he huffed, “Well, I would say the effort to dismantle the federal government was definitely that. Nobody voted for DOGE. Nobody voted to destroy the federal government in that manner.” Nobody votes for liberal EPA regulators either, but liberals love them. Nevertheless, Durán continued, “I think the disinformation being wrought by social media, which is only going to intensify, already is intensifying because of AI, is a massive threat to democracy because it's a battle over who controls reality and who believes what reality. And when we no longer have a common reality, that's when authoritarianism has its best chance of striking.” Like CBS, Comedy Central is a Skydance property. After the Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Stewart had his Daily Show contract extended through 2028, but Durán still hyperventilated, “Look at what Musk has been able to do with X or Twitter since he took over it, turn it into this sort of right-wing Nazi bar where he's the main algorithm in it, and now they're buying up other legacy media outlets. CBS is a goner. CNN is next. They're going to try to control reality, and I think that that is a hallmark of their anti-democratic vision.” CBS hasn’t changed dramatically under its new management, but even if it had, the idea that a less liberal CBS is a threat to democracy is itself anti-democratic. The same can be said for CNN, but Durán, the self-appointed guardian of democracy, is really upset that Musk allowed The Babylon Bee to start telling trans jokes on the platform. Later, Durán went full Marx, “You know, some people say we should nationalize these things. I agree with that in theory, but we'd have to pay these guys billions and billions of dollars to do that. I don't want them to get richer. We should seize whatever technologies are necessary to national security for the sake of national security, and we need to reset the relation between the public and the private sector when it comes to government, because obviously things have gotten way out of whack. Capitalism has declared war on democracy.” Even for Stewart, that may have been a bridge too far, “This is recognized, though, as you know, oligarchy and not — look reforms to capitalism, I think are always appropriate when it comes to reducing the friction in people's lives that, you know, for me, labor has been so mistreated over the past 50 or 60 years, and capital has been so fetishized that that helps create these great chasms of inequality that occur and makes you know average people's lives that much more difficult.” Stewart then wondered, “Are there less systemic change—you know, I'm still someone who's uncomfortable with seizing people's work. Are there narrower changes that can be made through the government that can tame an industry without whole hog, you know, just repossessing it?” Lefties are always bemoaning the size of the U.S. defense budget, but Durán’s proposal was to have the government fund its own alternatives, “Well, we could develop public versions of these things and fund those instead of funding private companies. I think— are you telling me that the United States of America doesn't know how to do surveillance? You know, doesn't know how to — I mean, we beat the Nazis, right? Why are we letting them now infiltrate and run our government? That's a big question, right? Why are we doing that?” Despite Stewart and Durán’s instance that democracy is whatever the opposite of what Elon Musk wants, Stewart still alleged, “You know, Musk will say this: ‘Oh, if Trump doesn't win, that's the end of our democracy. Oh, if we don't defeat DEI, that's the end of our democracy.’ They always paint democratic outcomes that they don't like as the end of democracy, but they never talk about the changes that they're making to the operating system of our country as in any way a threat to democracy.” If that isn’t the pot calling the kettle black, then nothing is. Still, missing the irony, Durán, again, went for the Nazi card, “Always accuse your enemy of that which you are actually doing. I forget which Nazi said that, but it's a fairly well known tactic.” Stewart mostly concurred, “You're big on the Nazis stuff, you know, and again, I like, I hate to be the guy tempering it, like, it's hard for me to go full Nazi on these guys, but I understand that it's certainly sometimes fascist adjacent if you really read what they're thinking of.” What about seizing property for running afoul of Durán’s ideology? Is that fascist? Here is a transcript for the November 18 show: Comedy Central The Weekly Show 11/18/2026 JON STEWART: This a purposeful threat to democracy, yes? Like, have they made specific moves that you consider, kind of, anti-democratic? You know, a sort of explicit revelation of their motivation. GIL DURAN: Well, I would say the effort to dismantle the federal government was definitely that. Nobody voted for DOGE. Nobody voted to destroy the federal government in that manner. In addition, they've, I think, made it pretty clear with their constant lies about the election, especially people like Elon Musk, that if Donald Trump were to declare the elections invalid, they'd be willing to go along with that. I think the disinformation being wrought by social media, which is only going to intensify, already is intensifying because of AI, is a massive threat to democracy because it's a battle over who controls reality and who believes what reality. And what we've seen so far is that, like, basically, the major use of AI is to create deep fakes on social media.
